coreTruths.title: Most patients hand you the diagnosis if you let them speak uninterrupted
coreTruths.broaderContext: History taking is the highest-yield diagnostic tool in dentistry. Get it right and the examination becomes confirmation. Get it wrong and even good investigations end up chasing the wrong question.
coreTruths.body:
## Patients run out of relevant story in 2-3 minutes

The instinct to fire a checklist of closed questions is wrong. Most patients hand over a working diagnosis if allowed to talk, and they typically lapse into silence after 2-3 minutes [1]. The clinician who interrupts at 30 seconds is the one who ends up taking a longer history.

## How questions are framed decides what the patient says next

Leading questions plant answers. Asking 'is the pain worse with hot drinks?' tells the patient what the right answer should be [2]. Open questions force the patient to describe their actual symptoms, which is what the differential needs. Leading questions are a tool kept for the reticent patient who will not volunteer detail otherwise [2].

## The character of the pain story is itself diagnostic

Patients with genuine organic pain usually describe it crisply when asked: sharp, throbbing, dull, aching. Patients whose pain has a strong behavioural overlay tend to be vague and prevaricate [3]. The way the story comes out is part of the data, not just background noise.

citations.quote: In fact, most patients will give the information necessary to make a provisional diagnosis, and further useful personal information, if allowed to speak uninterrupted. Most will lapse into silence after 2–3min of monologue.

Open questions should be used that require more than a simple ‘Yes’ or ‘No’ answer, to avoid leading the patient. Be careful of this when the question suggests the answer, e.g. ‘Is the pain worse when you drink hot drinks?’ However, with the more reticent patient it may be necessary to ask leading questions to elicit relevant information.

How would you describe the pain: sharp, shooting, dull, aching, etc.? This can be difficult, but patients with specific ‘organic’ pain will often understand exactly what you mean whereas patients with symptoms with a high behavioural overlay will be vague and prevaricate.

coreTruths.title: Sensibility testing tests the nerve, but pulp survival depends on blood supply
coreTruths.broaderContext: Vitality is a perfusion question, not a sensation question. Cold, heat, and electric pulp tests poke the nerve, which is a proxy. Knowing it is a proxy keeps the clinician from over-trusting a single result.
coreTruths.body:
## What the test actually measures

Cold, heat, and electric pulp testing all assess whether the nerve fibres respond. What actually keeps a pulp alive is its blood supply [1]. The test is a proxy. A traumatised tooth with intact circulation can give no response for months and still recover. A tooth with a normal response can have a compromised blood supply.

## Always test neighbours for comparison

A single number from one tooth means little. The same patient on the same day can react differently to the next tooth along. Test the suspect tooth and its neighbours so the response is calibrated to that patient [1].

## Heat response patterns separate non-vital from hyperaemic

No response to heat points to a non-vital tooth. An exaggerated, lingering response points to a hyperaemic, irreversibly inflamed pulp [2]. Same test, two very different diagnoses, depending on how the pulp reacts.

## Electric pulp readings are easily misread

The number on the EPT depends on battery strength and where the electrode sits on the tooth, not just the pulp [3]. Treat the reading as one piece of evidence, not a verdict. The test cavity, drilling into dentine without LA, is more definitive but destructive and reserved for last resort, mainly for crowned teeth [4].

citations.quote: It must be borne in mind when vitality testing that it is the integrity of the nerve supply that is being investigated. However, it is the blood supply which is of more relevance to the continued vitality of a pulp. Test the suspect tooth and its neighbours for comparison.
No response suggests that the tooth is non-vital, but an ↑ response indicates that the pulp is hyperaemic.

Most machines ascribe numbers to the patient’s reaction, but these should be interpreted with caution as the response can also vary with battery strength or the position of the electrode on the tooth.

Drilling into dentine without LA is an accurate diagnostic test, but as tooth tissue is destroyed it should only be used as a last resort. Can be helpful for crowned teeth but should be used with caution.

coreTruths.title: An investigation has no value unless the clinician can interpret and act on it
coreTruths.broaderContext: Tests, X-rays, and screening only help the patient if the result changes what happens next. Ordering investigations the clinician cannot read, or ignoring ones that have been done, is worse than not ordering them at all.
coreTruths.body:
## Don't request what you can't interpret

The rule is short: do not perform or request an investigation you cannot interpret [1]. A radiograph the clinician cannot read is irradiation without benefit. A blood test the clinician will not act on is a delay dressed up as a workup.

## Always look at, interpret, and act on results that come back

The other side of the same rule is that any investigation done must be looked at, interpreted, and acted on [2]. Ordering a test and not reading it is a medico-legal trap and a clinical one.

## Screening only helps if the practice can follow through

This applies to screening too. Measuring blood pressure on every adult in practice only helps if the clinician is trained in the technique, can avoid white-coat artefact, and can act meaningfully on a high reading [3]. Generating a queue of worried-well patients clogs the GP and helps no one. Catching real hypertension in a middle-aged man and getting it treated does [3].

citations.quote: Do not perform or request an investigation you cannot interpret.
Similarly, always look at, interpret, and act on any investigations you have performed.

What is crucial is that if you choose to initiate, say, a screening policy for hypertension in practice (i.e. you measure every adult’s blood pressure (BP)), you must ensure you are adequately trained in the technique, are aware of and avoid the risk of inducing disease (people get anxious at the dentist and may have ‘white coat hypertension’ which is of no significance), and act on significant results in a meaningful way. Generating a cohort of ‘worried well’ who then overload their GMP is hardly helpful whereas detecting significant hypertension in an unsuspecting middle-aged man who then has this corrected could be.

coreTruths.title: Diagnosis comes before treatment, and a differential comes before a definitive diagnosis
coreTruths.broaderContext: Treatment without a diagnosis is gambling. The whole point of history and examination is to narrow symptoms into a short list of possibilities that further tests can confirm or rule out.
coreTruths.body:
## The aim of the workup is a list of possibilities, not an answer

The goal of history and examination is not the final answer on the first visit. It is a provisional list: a few diagnoses ranked by likelihood [1]. From there, specific investigations earn their place by being able to confirm or refute one of the listed possibilities [2].

## The order matters: history, then preliminary tests, then differential, then specific tests

The sequence is not arbitrary. History and examination first, then preliminary investigations, then a differential, then specific investigations chosen because they discriminate between the items on that differential [2]. Skipping straight to a CBCT or a blood test before the differential exists is testing in the dark.

## A systematic exam is the safety net for distracted clinicians

When a clinician is rushed or thinking about the next patient, that is when pathology gets missed. A systematic, almost automatic, examination routine is what catches the lesion the clinician was not looking for [3]. The system is the insurance policy.

## The plan is a logical progression to oral health, not a list of fillings

The treatment plan is the logical sequence of steps to take the patient from where they are now to oral health, and then it gets carried out [4]. Real life rarely runs cleanly through the whole sequence, but the principle holds even when the plan has to be abbreviated [5].

citations.quote: The aim of this part of the history is to establish provisional differential diagnoses even before examining the patient.

Arriving at this stage is the whole point of taking a history and performing an examination, because by narrowing down your patient’s symptoms into possible diagnoses you can, in most instances, formulate a series of investigations &/or Rx that will benefit them.
The key to this is to develop a systematic approach, which becomes almost automatic, so that when you are under pressure there is less likelihood of missing any pathology.
List in a logical progression the steps which can be undertaken to take the patient to oral health.

This is the ideal, but life, as you are no doubt well aware, is far from ideal, and it is not always possible to follow this approach from beginning to end. The principles, however, remain valid and this general approach, even if much abbreviated, will help you deal with every new patient safely and sensibly.

coreTruths.title: Dental radiation risk is stochastic, not deterministic, so ALARP governs every exposure
coreTruths.broaderContext: There is no safe dose of ionising radiation when it comes to cancer induction. Doses in dentistry are too low to burn tissue, but every exposure adds incremental risk. That shapes how X-rays get justified.
coreTruths.body:
## Two kinds of radiation effect, only one applies in dentistry

Deterministic effects, like radiation burns, need a threshold dose that dentistry never gets near. Stochastic effects, like tumour induction, have no threshold. Any dose carries some probability of triggering a malignancy [1]. In dental imaging, stochastic risk is the only one that matters.

## Thyroid is the principal organ at risk

The thyroid is the head-and-neck organ most vulnerable to scatter from dental radiography [1]. That is why beam direction, collimation, and shielding decisions revolve around it.

## ALARP is the operating principle, not a slogan

ALARP, as low as reasonably practicable, is the rule for every exposure [1]. That cashes out as rectangular collimation, faster film (E speed cuts dose to half of D), the paralleling technique, and choosing the lowest-dose modality that answers the clinical question [2][3].

## Pregnancy does not change dental radiography unless the primary beam is on the fetus

With well-maintained, well-collimated equipment where the beam is not aimed at the gonads, risk is minimal. Pregnant patients get a lead apron if the primary beam is directed at the fetus, but otherwise are not treated differently [4]. The fear of irradiating a pregnant patient is usually larger than the actual risk from a routine intra-oral film.

citations.quote: There is no risk in dentistry of deterministic/certainty effects (e.g. radiation burns). Stochastic/change effects are more important (e.g. tumour induction). The thyroid is the principal organ at risk. Follow principles of ‘ALARP’ (as low as reasonably practicable) (…… Radiographs—the statutory regulations, p. 754).

Use a stationary anode (tungsten), direct current ↓ dose of self-rectifying machines. Direct action film (↑ detail) using D or E speed. E speed is double the speed of D hence ↓ dose to patient. Rectangular collimation ↓ unnecessary irradiation of tissues.

Paralleling technique: film is held in a film holder parallel to the tooth and the beam is directed (using a beam-aligning device) at right angles to the tooth and film. Focus-to-film distance is ↑ to minimize magnification; the optimum distance is 30cm. This is the most accurate and reproducible technique.

In well-maintained, well-collimated equipment where the beam does not point to the gonads, the risk of damage is minimal. Apply all normal principles to pregnant women (use a lead apron if the primary (p) beam is directed at the fetus), but otherwise do not treat any differently.
